articles.title: A British aunt left a £1 million estate to her niece and nephew, but a second will for her Cyprus flat threatened to bring 16 more relatives into the inheritance; a judge upheld the original English will
articles.summary: A high court judge has upheld an English will that leaves a £1 million estate to a niece and nephew.
articles.body: A high court judge has upheld an English will that leaves a £1 million estate to a niece and nephew. The judge rejected a challenge based on a later will made in Cyprus, which would have divided the assets among 18 relatives. The ruling, delivered in London, ends a complex international legal dispute between siblings Helen Thyer and Peter Crawford and their extended family. The estate belonged to their aunt, Dorothy Eirwen George, who died in 2021 at the age of 87. George was a retired teacher from Neath, Port Talbot. She had worked as a headmistress in Cyprus and still owned a flat in the coastal town of Peyia.The two wills and the Cypriot proceedingsGeorge made a valid English will in 2015. According to PA Media, she named her niece, Helen Thyer, as the sole executor and left her entire estate to Thyer and her brother, Peter Crawford. However, after her death, a second will came to light. It had been drawn up in Cyprus in 2019 and dealt only with the property she owned there. Under Cypriot forced heirship laws, this second will divided the flat among George’s 18 surviving relatives, rather than leaving it only to the people she had chosen. The 18 extended family members asked the UK courts to recognise the Cypriot will. They argued that it should take priority over the 2015 English will for the assets covered by the later document.The English court’s jurisdiction and decisionThe case went to the high court, where Judge Richard Spearman QC had to decide whether the two wills were valid and how they should apply. The main legal question was whether the 2019 Cypriot will cancelled the 2015 English will. Judge Spearman ruled that it did not. His decision was based on the exact wording of the Cypriot document. The judge found that the 2019 will did not include a clear clause cancelling all earlier wills. Instead, its wording suggested that it was meant to work alongside existing arrangements and apply only to the property in Cyprus. As the Cypriot will had no general clause cancelling previous wills, and was clearly intended to deal separately with property held abroad, the judge ruled that it was "not inconsistent" with the wider 2015 English will. As a result, the 2015 English will remains the main legal document covering Dorothy George’s entire worldwide estate, including the flat in Peyia.The consequences of the rulingThe high court’s decision means Helen Thyer and Peter Crawford will inherit the entire £1 million estate, in line with their aunt’s original wishes. The 18 other relatives who would have received a share under Cypriot forced heirship laws will get nothing from the UK estate. The ruling shows how complicated inheritance cases can become when someone owns property in different countries. Making separate wills for assets held in different countries can help simplify estate planning. However, the documents must be carefully written to avoid conflicts and prevent a later foreign will from causing legal disputes over the main estate. In this case, the Cypriot will did not clearly state that it cancelled the earlier English will. That detail proved decisive, allowing the two beneficiaries named in 2015 to keep their inheritance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Wife drugged and raped by husband asked police if she was to blame, court hears
articles.summary: The woman told a court suggestions she was 'pretending to be asleep' were 'absolute rubbish'.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A woman who had been drugged and raped by her husband for 20 years asked police: "Is it my fault he's done this?", a court heard.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, has admitted a litany of offences against her - including rape, administering a substance with intent and inviting 13 other men to join the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against her and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

Giving evidence in court for the first time, the woman also said claims she had been "pretending to be asleep" during the abuse were a "load of rubbish".

The victim, in her 60s, was formally interviewed by Greater Manchester Police on 7 November last year, around two weeks after officers had arrived at her family home to arrest her husband.

In the interview, played to the jury, she told Det Con Anouska Barker: "I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can't believe it's true, and I think you have made a mistake."

She told police at the time of her husband's arrest that as far as she knew, the pair had not had a sexual relationship for about nine years due to her experiencing symptoms of the menopause.

The husband, she said, had never complained about it and the pair never discussed it.

Asked how their sex life was before, the woman described it as "just normal, vanilla".

Asked by Barker what her husband had "been like" in the years they had not been in a sexual relationship, the woman said: "Is this my fault? Is it my fault that he has done this?"

"Absolutely not, I don't want you to ever think that," Barker replied.

Describing their relationship, she said they had been "a loving couple".

"We did things together, we went out with other people. We've always had quite a lot of friends and a good social circle and done things."

During the interviews she said she had never consented or agreed to anyone else being involved in their sex life, and it had never been suggested by her husband.

The woman said on a number of occasions she recalled feeling particularly "wobbly" and "weird" after drinking the previous night.

She told Barker she had messaged a friend to say: "I feel like I'm wasting the day and this is ridiculous, and I need to pull myself together and cook some dinner."

The woman said on one occasion in the summer of 2024, she felt so strange that friends suggested she "see a doctor".

Questioned about how much alcohol she drank, she said she would often drink a bottle of wine a night but was "usually fine" and would take herself to bed and remove her make-up, and would normally be up by 09:00.

Shown photographs of the men alleged to have abused her while she was unconscious, she told the detective she did not recognise any of them or remember speaking to them.

After the jury were shown the video of her police interviews, the woman was asked to take the stand in the courtroom.

Katy Thorne KC, representing 43-year-old paramedic Jonathan Kirk, said her client's case was that the victim had spoken to him and had her eyes open in the early hours of 17 August 2025 - when he allegedly raped her while she was unconscious in her bedroom.

Thorne said: "If I were to suggest to you - you were pretending to be asleep?"

The victim spoke calmly and directly and replied: "That's a load of rubbish is what I'd say."

Thorne said that Kirk's version of events was that the husband had explained that "you two as a couple had a sleep fetish; you had been pretending to sleep", asking the woman: "Is that something you recall?

Judge Maurice Greene interjected and asked: "Do you have a sleep fetish?"

The jury also heard another of the accused, taxi driver Philip Wild, claimed that the victim had "greeted him at the door" on the occasions he is alleged to have sexually assaulted and attempted to rape her, in August 2023 and February 2025 respectively.

In response to Pierce Power, defending Wild, she said: "No. That's a lie".

She was also questioned by the barrister representing Jordan Wallace, 31, who is alleged to have raped her on 4 May 2025.

Rachel White, defending Wallace, said she was not suggesting the victim had been "telling lies" but said she may have "not remembered" speaking to Wallace.

Counsel representing the other six men on trial did not ask questions.

Earlier in the trial Louise Oakley KC, prosecuting, said the woman had been subjected to the "barbaric fantasies" of her husband for more than two decades.

"The sad reality of this case is that there are many, many men whose fantasy is an unconscious and unresponsive woman," she said.

"[The husband] found a large number of them."

An investigation into his offending began after a team of undercover journalists in Germany infiltrated a channel on the messaging service Telegram which was being used by some men to share images of unconscious women appearing to be raped.

One of the users was traced by police to the husband's address, where he was arrested in October 2025.

Oakley said more than a million photographs and videos of his wife being abused were found on a Samsung mobile phone, which she described as a "confession booth" of his "darkest secrets".

On trial with alleged "contact offenders" Wild, Kirk and Wallace are amateur football coach Alan Keelan, 42; recruitment consultant Mohammed Sabir, 28; sheet metal worker Richard Townsend, 37, and Robert Stewart, 70, who was retired.

Also in the dock are Daniel Rayner and David Graves, described as alleged "non-contact offenders" because they did not physically attend the home address, who deny conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Four other men; Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee in Scotland; Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire, and non-contact offender Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset, have already pleaded guilty to a number of offences.

articles.title: Warren Buffett’s son Howard Buffett has visited Ukraine 27 times and committed $1.33 billion to the country; why he agreed to give $14 million when asked for just $1 million
articles.summary: Howard Buffett did not expect Ukraine to become one of the biggest priorities of his philanthropic work.
articles.body: Howard Buffett did not expect Ukraine to become one of the biggest priorities of his philanthropic work. But four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the billionaire farmer and philanthropist has committed an estimated $1.33 billion to the country through his foundation and visited it 27 times. His work spans agriculture, humanitarian aid, infrastructure, demining and rehabilitation.One decision, recounted in an interview with Forbes Ukraine, captures his approach. When the team behind Superhumans, a prosthetics and rehabilitation centre, approached him seeking $1 million, Buffett asked how much it would cost to build the entire facility. The answer was $14 million. His response: "Okay. We'll give you $14 million."The foundation's contribution to the project eventually grew to $77 million.Rebuilding a Ukrainian printing plant after a Russian attackBuffett first travelled to Ukraine in April 2022, at the suggestion of Shannon Sedgwick Davis, CEO of the Bridgeway Foundation. Initially unsure whether his organisation could make a meaningful difference, he changed his mind after meeting Ukrainians affected by the invasion.His foundation soon began funding organisations involved in documenting war crimes, distributing food and providing humanitarian assistance.One major intervention followed a Russian missile attack on Factor-Druk, a printing plant in Kharkiv. The facility printed around one in every three Ukrainian books and was the country's largest producer of Ukrainian-language school textbooks. The attack killed seven people and injured 21.Buffett's foundation financed its reconstruction, which took nine months and cost $8.9 million. The company selected contractors and equipment, while the foundation paid the bills directly. The aim was not just to restore a business but also to protect access to Ukrainian-language textbooks.Why he bought agricultural machinery for Ukrainian farmersAgriculture became another priority. The war damaged machinery, contaminated farmland and prevented farmers from accessing their fields, threatening a sector crucial to global food supplies.During his first visit, Buffett contacted John Deere's president to ask how many tractors and combine harvesters were available in Europe. Fifteen machines originally destined for Russia had been left available after deliveries were halted."I'll take them all," Buffett replied.He also bought available combines from New Holland. The purchases became part of Victory Harvest, a programme that provides small and medium-sized Ukrainian farms with free access to agricultural machinery.The foundation invested more than $60 million in equipment. Between 2022 and 2025, it helped cultivate 823,000 hectares of farmland through 3,636 requests. Farmers also saved almost $25 million in rental costs between 2022 and 2024, according to programme estimates.His focus on demining technology has drawn criticismUkraine has estimated that 17.4 million hectares could be contaminated with mines and unexploded ordnance. Buffett's foundation initially supported demining organisations, including the HALO Trust, before backing new technology to make land safe.This included the GAR-3100, an autonomous tractor fitted with heavy rollers, and the GAR-5120, a mechanised demining vehicle.However, his approach has also attracted criticism. Some in the sector believe the focus on developing new machines can come at the expense of sustained funding for existing teams. The foundation rejected a request to support 50 trained deminers, and the Canadian government eventually stepped in to save the team.The $14 million donation that grew to $77 millionSuperhumans, which provides prosthetics, rehabilitation and treatment for people injured in the war, remains one of Buffett's most prominent projects.When co-founder Andrey Stavnitser's team initially sought $1 million, Buffett's team asked how much it would cost to build the entire facility. After being told $14 million, he agreed to fund it.The foundation's contribution has since reached $77 million towards the Lviv campus, its operations and prosthetic care. Buffett has also encouraged the organisation to develop fundraising sources beyond his foundation so it does not become dependent on a single donor.Where the foundation's $1.33 billion has goneThe high-profile projects account for less than a quarter of the foundation's total commitment. Its spending also includes:- $351 million on food assistance: More than 642.9 million meals have been funded. A kitchen in Bucha provides meals to nearly 7,500 schoolchildren daily.- $244 million on strategic infrastructure: Includes the Factor-Druk reconstruction, more than 344,000 replacement windows, nine bridges, four power plants, school shelters and over 2,500 generators.- $125 million on war-crimes documentation: Includes funding for 18 DNA laboratories for Ukrainian police.- $103 million on public safety: Covers ambulances, emergency radios, 240 working dogs and equipment for Kyiv's Okhmatdyt children's hospital.- $53 million for young people: Includes 54 children's centres that have served more than two million children, along with camps and other programmes.The foundation works through around 50 partners, including international organisations, Ukrainian non-profits and public institutions.Who is Howard Buffett?At 71, Howard is the middle child of investor Warren Buffett. A farmer since 1977, he manages 1,600 acres in central Illinois and served as sheriff of Macon County from 2017 to 2018. He has also served on Berkshire Hathaway's board for 33 years and became its chairman on September 18, 2026. Greg Abel remains the company's CEO.A photographer and author of eight books, Howard has documented the destruction and resilience he has witnessed in Ukraine. His visits have also become personal: he has attended family occasions and once travelled from the United States for just two days to keep a promise to attend the wedding of two Ukrainian service members.Buffett has said his experiences in Ukraine changed his outlook. He has praised the resourcefulness of its people while also expressing concern that corruption could hold back the country's economic potential.His foundation plans to keep supporting agriculture, demining and Superhumans, including a greater focus on farming practices such as no-till agriculture in the post-war period. Under Warren Buffett's plan, the foundation is scheduled to cease operations by 2045.The $1.33 billion committed to Ukraine is expected to approach $1.5 billion by the end of 2026. Buffett has credited the results not only to his foundation but also to the Ukrainians who helped turn its support into tangible work."That is just as much a credit to the people we have met in Ukraine," he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: All bark no bite: Do 'lame duck' Donald Trump's tariff threats carry weight anymore?
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed fresh tariffs on 14 major US trading partners, citing concerns over \"excess industrial capacity\" and its
articles.body: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed fresh tariffs on 14 major US trading partners, citing concerns over "excess industrial capacity" and its adverse impact on American commerce.The proposed measures follow an eight-month investigation conducted by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The investigation examined alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.The countries and trading blocs targeted by the proposed tariffs include China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.But with Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, can US President Donald Trump still push ahead with his tariff plans?What gives Trump the power to impose tariffsThe US Constitution gives Congress the authority to impose taxes and regulate foreign trade under Article I, Section 8. However, Congress has passed several laws relinquishing specific trade-related powers to the President, allowing the executive to impose tariffs under certain circumstances.Trump's latest tariff proposals are based on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 which allows the US administration to take action against foreign countries whose policies or practices are found to be unfair and to burden or restrict American commerce.Unlike legislation passed by Congress, Section 301 action does not require a fresh vote by lawmakers. However, the administration must follow the investigation, consultation and decision-making procedures laid down under the law.What can Democrats do to challenge Trump's tariff plansOn January 3, 2027, Democrats will take control of both chambers, giving them several avenues to challenge Trump's tariff agenda.They could introduce legislation to restrict or narrow the President's authority to impose tariffs.They could hold congressional hearings and investigate the administration's tariff decisions.They could use their control over federal spending and legislative proceedings to put pressure on the administration.However, any legislation seeking to limit Trump's tariff powers would face a presidential veto. Overriding it would require a two-thirds majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, making bipartisan support necessary.Can the Supreme Court stop Trump againThe Supreme Court has already ruled against one of Trump's major tariff strategies.On February 20, the court ruled 6-3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not give the President the authority to impose tariffs. The ruling struck down the administration's use of emergency powers to levy sweeping import duties.However, the decision does not prevent Trump from using other laws that specifically delegate trade powers to the executive branch.Businesses and other affected parties could, however, challenge the new tariffs in court if they believe the administration has exceeded its legal authority or failed to comply with the statutory procedures.The Supreme Court could ultimately be asked to examine such challenges, although the outcome would depend on the legal grounds and facts of each case.You use AI every day. articles.title: EU deal will 'give back some rights' lost to Brexit
articles.summary: Paul Ingrouille says the UK-EU deal may ease up "onerous" trade processes.
articles.body:
Some business and political leaders have predicted how a new deal for a closer working relationship with the EU could bring "simplified" trade, more study opportunities, and a boost to the workforce in the Channel Islands.

The agreement between the UK and the EU , expected for 2028, would "give back some of the rights" from before Brexit, while requiring changes to "more than 100" regulations said Deputy Kirsten Morel, Jersey's Assistant Minister for Environment, Agriculture and Fisheries.

Earlier in November, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was " madness " for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to make Brexit his "political priority".

Sir Mark Boleat, Jersey Senator and Minister for Planning and Regulation, said some people in the Channel Islands with "notions of complete independence" had supported Brexit - but stressed it was "never the political issue" it was in the UK because they were not in the European Union and had no vote.

Boleat said Jersey was not part of the single market and made its money largely "from selling financial services" - which he said was not impacted by leaving the EU.

Regarding the new deal, he said while the number of students who would benefit from study opportunities would be "quite small" - trade could benefit, particularly within the fishing industry.

It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme .

From March 2028, most checks on food, fish and agricultural goods moving between the UK, EU and Crown Dependencies are set to end.

Paul Ingrouille, a plant seller in Guernsey, said simplified trade legislation could put businesses like his in a "better position to be competitive in Europe".

Ingrouille, manager at Guernsey Clematis, an international wholesale exporter of young plants to countries including mainland Europe, said the business currently had to adhere to "quite strict requirements" - including having plants checked by inspectors.

Describing the process as "onerous", he said it had been less so before Brexit, and that it now took up more time and cost - especially when dealing with a batch of up to 100,000 plants.

He said the new deal could "simplify" this process through the return of a "plant passport system" allowing smoother transit across European borders.

It could also be beneficial to the breeding of new varieties of clematis, he said - while currently they had to register the trademark both in Britain and Europe, this could be "harmonised" across both jurisdictions.

This would enable the company to be in "a better position to be competitive in Europe".

Aqua-Mar, a Jersey-based family run business that specialises in shellfish, said there was a "bigger conversation" to be had when it came to the fishing industry.

Voicing a fear the firm would not be viable by the time the deal was brokered in 2028, a spokesperson said Brexit had contributed to issues including a decline in "locally available stocks" and the cost of transport and operation.

"Making it easier to export is one thing, but we need to have something to export in the first place," they said - noting they were now importing stock to sustain the business.

They said: "The challenges we are facing are immediate, and I fear that by the time these changes come into effect, much of the infrastructure that supports the local fishing industry may already have been lost."

Meanwhile, Morel said Brexit had been "most keenly felt" by fishers, who have had to export their goods via Saint-Malo - rather than Granville in Normandy, as before.

"We spent five years working with France and Europe to get a new inspection post open in Granville," he said - which would now only be in use for 18 months.

Describing Brexit as a "chastening experience" for Jersey, he said leaders should seek to negotiate with the EU and the UK and "have its relationship with Europe in its control", while also maintaining a relationship with the UK.

He said the latest agreements would affect "more than 100" regulations which were changed after Brexit - requiring "juggling" between the government, law drafters and the States to take advantage of the new agreements.

The deal would also allow islanders aged 18 to 31 to live, work, volunteer and study in the EU for two years and Channel Islands' students studying at UK higher education settings will be able to study in Europe.

"Youth mobility" would be a "huge advantage", said Morel, with university places abroad more easily accessible.

Although he said the "cultural impact" of Brexit would remain - citing the departure from Jersey of European people who had become residents - he said Jersey always needed to have "clear connections" with Europe.

Deputy Steve Falla, member of the Policy and Resources Committee for the States of Guernsey, described the deal as "very good news" which would likely lead to a "reduction in the friction in trade we do with Europe".

He said this was particularly important for trade relations with France.

"The team who work with me have done so much good work ensuring Guernsey's interests and needs and position are properly understood by those in the UK doing the negotiations."

He said Brexit had "an adverse effect" in Guernsey - leading to more paperwork in trade, while having a detrimental effect on the workforce.

While the deal would not "reverse" Brexit, he said he believed it would benefit the island.

Ruby Swaisland, who now works in Guernsey, said she had a "great experience" studying abroad in Amsterdam.

She said this had "broadened her perspective" on the world, while she thought it was "a shame" that those opportunities were "cut off" by Brexit.

Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

While Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the move by Burnham was "trying to take Britain back... instead of focusing on the future".

The UK voted to leave the European Union on 23 June 2016.

The Channel Islands were not eligible to vote because they were self-governing Crown Dependencies - not part of the United Kingdom and never members of the European Union.

Shortly afterwards, there were surveys in Guernsey and Jersey to gain insight into the views of islanders o Brexit.

In Guernsey, 60% of the 1,610 respondents to the Island Global Research Survey said they would have voted Remain.

Meanwhile, in 2017, a survey of 800 residents in Jersey found "many islanders" were "concerned that Jersey's interests will not be adequately represented in the UK's negotiations with the EU".

Ammar Ebrahim, BBC Jersey political reporter, said as the islands had never been a member of the European Union, they "historically occupied a halfway house called Protocol 3".

"Under this protocol the islands had access to the single market which came with trade benefits for agricultural and fishing but most EU rules including those on finance, taxation and free movement of people did not apply to the islands.

"After the UK voted to leave the EU in 2016 the next step was for the UK government to negotiate a new deal with the EU which it did in 2020 through the UK-EU trade and co-operation agreement.

"Jersey and Guernsey were given a choice of whether or not to participate in the agreement, and at emergency States sittings in late 2020 - just days after Christmas - politicians voted in favour of doing so. The agreement has since then governed the islands' new relationship with the EU.

"This meant more bureaucracy through more paperwork and border checks for goods which created difficulty for farming and fishing sectors.

"There is now cautious optimism following this new deal between the UK and EU which has been seen as an effort by Burnham to move away from a hard Brexit. It seems in the political world in Jersey the deal is unanimously seen as a positive step.

"While the UK's relationship with the EU continues to generate strong opinions on both sides of the debate in the UK, the political reality in the Channel Islands is different. There has never been a strong Brexit feeling here, largely because the islands relationship with the EU never generated the frustrations that it did on the mainland.

"However, there remains a worry that the islands are not in charge of their own destiny when it comes to their relationship with the EU and while this new deal seems promising on paper for fishing, agriculture and opportunities for young people, there is a sense that people want to know more details about how these changes will work in practice."

articles.title: PM Modi asks ministers to stay put & stay ready; next Parliament session likely before December 15: Report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has reportedly asked his ministerial colleagues to complete preparations for the next session of Parliament before
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has reportedly asked his ministerial colleagues to complete preparations for the next session of Parliament before December 15 and avoid foreign travel in the run-up to it, signalling that the government wants ministers to remain available ahead of the sitting.The issue of the upcoming session figured at Wednesday's Cabinet meeting chaired by PM Modi, according to sources cited by news agency PTI.The prime minister suggested that the session be convened before December 15 and asked ministers to ensure that their respective ministries were ready.The Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs will take the final call on the commencement date and duration of the session, the sources said.The preparations come amid questions from opposition parties over the delay in convening the Winter Session. As of Wednesday night, the Monsoon Session remained unprorogued, more than 100 days after both Houses were adjourned indefinitely on August 13.The absence of an announcement on the next sitting has also fuelled speculation about a possible special session, particularly in connection with the proposed delimitation of Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies.Delimitation Bill likely to be a key testWith Parliament expected to meet before December 15, attention is on whether the government will bring the proposed Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, linked to delimitation and women's reservation.The legislation failed to secure the required numbers during a special sitting of Parliament on April 17. Its passage would require a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha, amounting to 361 votes in the present 543-member House. With three vacancies, the House currently has 540 members.The ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) has 320 members and would need support from opposition parties to reach the threshold.The political arithmetic has changed since the Bill's defeat, with 26 MPs having moved out of the opposition camp. 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs broke away and merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), pledging support to the NDA, while six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs joined the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena.Despite these developments, the government would still need additional support. The DMK, with 22 Lok Sabha MPs, and the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), with eight, could play a significant role in the numbers game.The government is also learnt to be considering a formula under which Lok Sabha seats would be increased by 50% across states to address concerns, particularly among southern states, over the implications of delimitation.The proposed framework is understood to retain the existing inter-state share of seats based on the 1971 Census. However, no final decision has been taken.Opposition questions delay, raises concerns over delimitationThe delay in announcing the next parliamentary sitting has drawn criticism from the Congress, which has questioned the government's intentions and sought clarity on its plans for delimitation.Congress spokesperson Jairam Ramesh said the country should have been informed by now about the dates of either the Winter Session or a possible special sitting."What games are being played by the PM-HM jodi, assuming that the jodi is still together?" Ramesh asked, referring to PM Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah.He also questioned the government's approach to securing the numbers for the proposed legislation and demanded details of its delimitation formula."By now having seen (through) the desperate efforts of the jodi to cobble together a super-tainted two-thirds majority in Lok Sabha, the nation is entitled to know what the PM-HM formula for delimitation is, assuming that there is indeed one," he said.Ramesh further alleged that the uncertainty surrounding Parliament and the Bill suggested that "there is something truly sinister that is being planned".Opposition parties are also expected to raise their objections to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar during the upcoming session.A ruling alliance MP told PTI that debate and voting on a Constitution amendment Bill would not be possible unless the House functioned in an orderly manner.The government faces procedural constraints as well: an extended sitting of the existing session requires at least two days' notice, while convening a fresh session requires a minimum notice of 14 days.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US senator Cory Booker seeks answers from Nvidia over Jensen Huang's return, raises antitrust concerns
articles.summary: Senator Cory Booker raises antitrust concerns over Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang's return amid national security questions and potential corporate influence.
articles.body: US Senator Cory Booker has sought an explanation from Nvidia over the circumstances surrounding CEO Jensen Huang's return to the company, questioning whether the chipmaker's growing influence has made it too powerful to face accountability.In a letter sent to Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones on Wednesday, the New Jersey Democrat requested details of communications between the Trump administration and the company's board before Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement, according to a letter seen by Reuters.Booker also questioned President Donald Trump's assurances that Huang did not pose a national security threat. He asked Nvidia to preserve board records relating to the leadership decision and provide details of an independent investigation into the company's compliance with US export controls.Booker is the top Democrat on the Senate antitrust subcommittee and is expected to lead it when the next Congress begins in January. His intervention signals that Nvidia's market dominance and its business connections with China could face greater scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers.Huang stepped down from his leadership position on November 12 following reports of alleged extramarital affairs, including claims involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Trump subsequently called for his return, and Nvidia reinstated him on Monday.The developments triggered sharp movements in financial markets. Nvidia shares rose more than 31% following Huang's reinstatement after technology stocks had initially fallen amid the uncertainty. However, the company's stock dropped 8% in early US trading on Wednesday.Booker argued that the episode raised questions about the extent of Nvidia's influence over the economy and whether its leadership had become too important for the government to hold accountable."The antitrust laws exist to prevent this kind of concentration where a company is so dominant that a mere change in its leadership threatens household savings and the broader economy," he wrote in the letter.The senator also questioned the Trump administration's involvement in Huang's return, arguing that the episode highlighted concerns about the concentration of corporate power.The issue has drawn attention from other lawmakers as well, with congressional committees preparing to question Huang about the company's operations and its links to China.According to the Reuters report, Huang is expected to appear before the House Intelligence Committee in a closed-door session on December 1. He is also scheduled to attend a public hearing of the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.Booker said the Senate antitrust subcommittee had grounds to examine Nvidia's position in the market and what he described as the federal government's treatment of its leadership as indispensable to the economy.You use AI every day. articles.title: PRAGATI meeting: PM Modi reviews infrastructure projects worth over Rs 78,000 crore, stresses timely execution
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday reviewed five critical infrastructure projects worth more than Rs 78,000 crore across the road,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday reviewed five critical infrastructure projects worth more than Rs 78,000 crore across the road, railway, power and coal sectors, directing ministries and state governments to resolve pending issues with clear responsibilities and realistic timelines.The review took place at the 55th meeting of PRAGATI, an ICT-enabled platform that brings together the Centre and state governments to monitor projects, address implementation bottlenecks and improve the delivery of public schemes.PM Modi emphasised that delays in infrastructure projects have consequences beyond cost escalation, as they also postpone the benefits meant for citizens, businesses and the economy.He stressed that timely execution must go hand in hand with high construction standards.“Projects worth over Rs 78,000 crore reviewed in today’s PRAGATI session. Sectors covered are roads, railways, power and coal,” the prime minister said in a post on X.The meeting also included an extensive review of the Industrial Training Institute (ITI) ecosystem and the implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU) initiative, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office.Focus on infrastructure delivery and power supplyDuring the review of road projects, PM Modi called for faster implementation and reiterated the need to focus on outcomes rather than merely expenditure.For coal projects, he stressed that rehabilitation and resettlement should be carried out in a timely and dignified manner alongside project execution.In the power sector, the prime minister suggested exploring innovative models for decentralised solar and wind energy projects. He said such projects should, wherever feasible, be developed closer to consumption centres, taking into account local resource availability and demand.According to the PMO statement, the approach is intended to improve access to reliable and affordable electricity while reducing pressure on transmission infrastructure.PM calls for stronger industry-ITI partnershipsA significant part of the meeting focused on strengthening the ITI ecosystem and implementing PM-SETU.PM Modi called on chief ministers and chief secretaries to take the lead in upgrading ITIs and encouraging greater industry participation. He said the industry had an opportunity to partner with these institutes, contribute to their modernisation and align training with current and future workforce requirements.He also called for closer collaboration between state governments, ITIs and industry to improve training and employment opportunities for young people.Public sector undertakings (PSUs) were asked to assess their future manpower requirements and strengthen links with ITIs to facilitate training and recruitment in relevant trades. The prime minister also encouraged them to support practical training and apprenticeships and increase the intake of trained ITI graduates.Such partnerships would give students industry experience while helping PSUs access a pool of skilled workers suited to their operational requirements, the PMO statement said.‘Classroom, company and career’ approachPM Modi stressed that skill development should be organised around industrial clusters and the requirements of individual sectors. He called for ITI trades, curricula and training capacity to be aligned with existing industries and upcoming investments in different regions.He said stronger connections between ITIs and local employers could create more employment opportunities closer to home, reduce distress-driven migration and allow young people to contribute to the economic development of their regions.The prime minister also advocated a ‘classroom’, ‘company’ and ‘career’ (3C) approach to ITI education, linking classroom learning with practical industry experience and, subsequently, employment and career progression.He emphasised that ITIs and companies should work together to equip students with relevant technical knowledge, exposure to actual workplace conditions and a clear pathway from training to employment.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Cheeni Kum: Poor monsoon hits sugar crop, gross output may not meet domestic need
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India’s gross sugar production is estimated to decline 15% in the 2026-27 season (Oct-Sept), the lowest level in a decade, primarily due to a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s gross sugar production is estimated to decline 15% in the 2026-27 season (Oct-Sept), the lowest level in a decade, primarily due to a sharp fall in output in Maharashtra and Karnataka following deficient rainfall, as per industry body ISMA.However, the decline in net sugar availability is expected to be relatively lower at 5.4%, as govt has stopped diversion of sugar for ethanol production during the current season. Net sugar production is estimated at around 265 lakh tonne, as against nearly 280 lakh tonne in the previous season. Data show that in the last decade, net sugar production was the lowest at 202.5 lakh in 2016-17 and second lowest at 261 lakh tonne in 2024-25.The difference between gross and net sugar production is essentially the quantity of sugar diverted for ethanol manufacturing. With no such diversion allowed this season, the entire estimated output will be available for domestic consumption.India’s annual sugar consumption is pegged at 280-285 lakh tonne. The projected production, therefore, falls short of domestic demand, potentially putting pressure on retail prices and increasing the possibility of further imports to meet any supply shortfall.In a statement, Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said weather conditions across major sugar-producing states had varied, with crop development affected by El Niño-related climate variability, unseasonal rainfall, prolonged dry spells and crop lodging in certain regions.“The impact of uneven rainfall, prolonged dry spells and crop lodging in certain regions has been reflected in the current assessment,” said Deepak Ballani, director general of ISMA.Among states, Uttar Pradesh is projected to remain the largest producer at 89 lakh tonne, followed by Maharashtra at 87 lakh tonne and Karnataka at 46.2 lakh tonne.Govt data showed that the average retail price of sugar stood at Rs 61 per kg on Tuesday, 31% higher than a year ago.On Wednesday, the govt extended the deadline for duty-free imports of 10 lakh tonne of raw sugar to March 31, 2027. In a separate notification, it also extended the deadline for converting imported raw sugar into white or refined sugar and selling it in the domestic market to Sept 30, 2027.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An AI security camera mistook a Maryland teenager’s bag of Doritos for a gun; armed police detained four students, who are now suing the school district and AI company
articles.summary: A bag of Doritos was all one teenager had in his hands while waiting outside his school after football practice.
articles.body: A bag of Doritos was all one teenager had in his hands while waiting outside his school after football practice. But an artificial intelligence-powered security camera interpreted the packet as a firearm, setting off a chain of events that brought several armed police officers to the Maryland school. Four teenagers were ordered to their knees, handcuffed and searched, even though the alert had already been cancelled after officials identified the object as a bag of crisps. Now, the students are taking legal action against their school district, the surveillance technology company and others, alleging that a preventable technology error led to an unlawful police encounter.How a packet of Doritos triggered a police response outside Kenwood High SchoolAs reported by Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, the incident dates back to October 20, 2025, when four students were spending time outside Kenwood High School in Baltimore County, Maryland, after football practice. According to a civil rights complaint, Taki Allen was eating Cool Ranch Doritos that had been handed out by his coach. The other three students, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr. and Keith Winfield III, were with him.The school district was using Omnilert Gun Detect, an AI-based weapons detection system connected to its existing security cameras. Shortly before 7:04 pm, the software identified the packet in Allen's hand as a possible firearm, assigning the image a 90% confidence score. The alert was then passed on to the company's human review team, which also failed to identify the object correctly and forwarded the warning to school personnel.The first response from school safety officials and a Baltimore County police sergeant was different. After examining the footage, they recognised that the supposed weapon was actually a bag of chips. The alert was cancelled within approximately two minutes of being generated, according to the lawsuit. A cancellation message was sent to the original recipients, while the system's online dashboard also reflected that the warning had been withdrawn.How a cancelled AI alert still led to six police cruisers arriving at the schoolThe complaint alleges that Kenwood High School principal Catherine 'Kate' Smith subsequently looked at the original image without taking account of the cancellation notice. Reportedly, more than 10 minutes after the alert had been withdrawn, she reportedly sent a screenshot to the school's resource officer. In a message to other administrators at around 7:19 pm, Smith allegedly indicated that the person shown in the image was still outside the school and appeared to be armed. The resource officer then passed the screenshot to Baltimore County police. Officers were dispatched at approximately 7:21 pm to investigate a report of someone carrying a weapon.At least six police vehicles arrived, according to the filing. Several officers approached with their firearms drawn. The four teenagers raised their hands, but were instructed to get down on their knees. They were handcuffed and subjected to searches of their bodies and belongings. The lawsuit maintains that none of the students had behaved suspiciously or committed an offence. Three of them, it says, were not even visible in the original image that had triggered the AI alert.When Thompson questioned why he was being detained, an officer allegedly explained that he was being held because he had been with Allen. The complaint reproduces the officer's response as, 'You were just with him, ok, so guilty by association if you want to say that.'Police discovered the supposed weapon was a packet of chipsThe searches produced no firearms. Officers subsequently examined the original surveillance image and compared it with empty Doritos packets found in a nearby rubbish bin. The object identified by the software was confirmed to be a bag of crisps. The complaint says one officer acknowledged that the AI system had mistaken the food packaging for a gun. As the officers prepared to leave, another reportedly expressed frustration with the surveillance equipment, referring to the cameras as 'stupid AI cameras'.There was also an exchange that the students' lawyers have included in their account of what happened afterwards. The supervising officer, Corporal Michael Foehrkolb, allegedly thanked the teenagers for not running away, adding that doing so would have created a serious problem.The complaint also describes the physical and emotional effects of the encounter. The students say they were frightened as officers approached with guns, unsure whether even a sudden movement might put them in greater danger. Their handcuffs reportedly left marks and caused pain. Thompson also told officers that the restraints were aggravating an existing wrist injury, but the complaint alleges that his concerns were not addressed by loosening them. The consequences did not end when the police left. The teenagers describe anxiety around law enforcement and discomfort about remaining on school grounds after normal activities. Allen, who is still a student at Kenwood, reportedly began arranging paid rides home rather than waiting outside the building after practice.Four students take school district and AI company to court over false gun alertThe filing also refers to messages exchanged between Smith and the school resource officer after it became clear that the object was not a firearm. In one exchange described in the complaint, the officer reportedly explained that it was a 'bag of chips not a gun', adding a laughing emoji. Smith allegedly responded with 'Bwahahaha'. The students argue that the response points to wider problems in the way the school handled the incident. Their complaint is not limited to the AI system's inability to distinguish food packaging from a weapon. It also questions why a warning that had already been withdrawn was allowed to prompt a police deployment.The civil rights action was filed on November 17, 2026, in Baltimore County Circuit Court. The four plaintiffs are represented by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, alongside Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP and Engel Law Group, P.C.The defendants named in the case include Omnilert LLC, Baltimore County Public Schools, Baltimore County, school administrators and individual police officers. The claims include alleged violations of the Fourth and 14th Amendments, protections under the Maryland Constitution, false imprisonment and negligence. These are allegations presented in the complaint and have not been established through a court ruling.How repeated false gun alerts raised questions about AI surveillance in schoolsThe case also brings attention to the scale at which the school district had adopted automated weapons detection. According to the complaint, Baltimore County Public Schools introduced Omnilert Gun Detect across 165 schools between autumn 2023 and spring 2024. The technology was connected to more than 7,000 security cameras already operating across the district.The system is marketed as a way to identify firearms through surveillance footage while distinguishing them from everyday objects. However, the students' lawyers cite findings from Maryland's Office of the Inspector General for Education indicating that more than 99% of the alerts produced by the system in Baltimore County schools were false positives that did not require police intervention.The complaint also refers to previous police responses to alerts involving objects that were not guns. These allegedly included children's toys, a stapler and a glue gun. The plaintiffs argue that repeated problems should have prompted stronger procedures for reviewing warnings and ensuring that cancelled alerts reached everyone who might act on them.They further allege that the district did not provide sufficient training or establish a reliable method of communicating cancellations to school administrators and law enforcement personnel. In their account, the October 2025 detention was connected not only to a mistaken identification but also to failures in the handling of information after the mistake had been recognised. Omnilert reportedly maintained after the incident that its process had functioned as intended.Students seek changes to school security and police proceduresDamon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said the students had been let down by both the technology and the adults responsible for responding to the alert. He argued that automated systems could create serious problems when officials rely on their warnings without properly checking the information or coordinating with one another.Leah Frazier, director of the organisation's Digital Justice Initiative, also raised concerns about the use of AI surveillance around young people. She said safeguards and clear expectations for the adults handling these systems were necessary as their use expanded in schools and other public settings.Freida Winfield, the mother of student Keith Winfield III, described the experience from a parent's perspective. She questioned why her son had been exposed to an armed police response while simply waiting outside his school for a ride home.The plaintiffs are seeking financial compensation as well as court-ordered changes to the way AI-generated security alerts are handled. Their requests include proper verification before police are dispatched, effective communication when an alert is cancelled, improved staff training and greater oversight of the technology's performance.They are also calling for more transparency and community involvement in decisions about the use of AI surveillance in schools. According to the complaint, Omnilert Gun Detect remains in operation at Kenwood High School, while the students maintain that the shortcomings that contributed to their detention have not been adequately addressed.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports by The New York Times and a civil rights lawsuit filed by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. The Times of India has not independently verified the allegations made in the complaint.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: BBC appeals against decision to allow Trump's $10bn lawsuit to go ahead
articles.summary: The US president is suing the BBC over the way Panorama edited a speech he gave in 2021.
articles.body:
The BBC has lodged an "urgent" appeal against a US judge's decision to allow Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the corporation to go ahead.

The US president is suing the BBC for defamation over the way an episode of Panorama edited a speech he gave in January 2021, shortly before the riot at the US Capitol.

Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that the defamation case could proceed after the BBC sought to dismiss it.

The BBC has now filed an appeal with a higher court, saying there is a "complete lack of evidence" that anyone in Florida accessed the programme, and that the broadcaster made "rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary" in the US.

A BBC spokesman said: "We are surprised and disappointed by the court's decision that this case should be heard in Florida.

"As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK - and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.

"Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling."

President Trump's lawsuit accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for the edit in Trump: A Second Chance, which it said had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

But the corporation argued that the Panorama episode, which was broadcast in 2024, did not meet the legal criteria for defamation.

Earlier this month, federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not rule on the merits of the case.

President Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a post on Truth Social at the time.

The BBC has now lodged an appeal with the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, arguing that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.

Trump has been ordered to answer questions under oath as part of the lawsuit by 22 January.

Judge Kuntz has scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

articles.title: Nigel Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU
articles.summary: The Reform UK leader reunites with businessman Arron Banks in support of the Keep Britain Out campaign.
articles.body:
Nigel Farage has helped launch a new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union.

The Reform UK leader offered his support to Keep Britain Out, which sees him reunite with his Brexit-supporting ally Arron Banks - who co-founded the Leave.EU campaign during the 2016 referendum.

Farage was the first MP to sign the campaign's "Pledge for Britain". This contains "10 commitments" for elected officials to abide by, including opposing rejoining the EU, its single market or customs union.

The campaign was launched as Prime Minister Andy Burnham explores closer ties with the EU, after he agreed a deal with the bloc covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" and has suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

But he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

On Monday, Burnham said there was "no fixed destination" on the talks with the EU, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Farage said the 2016 referendum was the "most divisive thing I have seen in families, in communities" and he hopes the next general election "kills this stone dead".

He told reporters: "I didn't pick this fight, the prime minister has picked this fight. As far as I was concerned it was done and dusted.

"But if battle has to be joined I will join it gleefully. What he's doing is madness, it's not necessary."

Farage said Keep Britain Out would be a "forward-looking, positive campaign about how Britain can be richer, more productive" outside the EU.

There are 10 issues listed on the pledge card, including asking signatories to "oppose mass migration" and support the country's farming and fishing industries.

Farage suggested he expects other Reform MPs and candidates to sign the pledges.

Banks said he wants pro-leave MPs to support them, adding: "We hope some Labour MPs will see sense and sign it and even Conservatives."

Asked if he is funding the campaign and to what extent, Banks said a "whole series of donors" have been "back in touch".

He added: "The last campaign was also funded by the British public, so I'm not going to go into who's donating what at this stage."

The launch of Keep Britain Out follows the formation of another anti-EU campaign called Stay Out , which has received support from Lord Gove - the chairman of the Vote Leave campaign in 2016.

Meanwhile, the European Movement is helping launch a rival campaign to rejoin the EU, called Get In.

articles.title: US Army says controlled lead azide explosives blast in Iowa was 'huge success'
articles.summary: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
articles.body:
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

President Donald Trump said reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

"We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.

Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.

He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.

"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.

Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.

The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.

"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.

"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."

Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.

"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.

Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"

Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".

Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".

Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.

In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.

It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.

The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.

But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.

Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

articles.title: Vanity Fair piece on Taylor Swift that doesn't mention her by name draws criticism
articles.summary: Vanity Fair's no-names Taylor Swift exposé "The Mastermind" ignited a journalism debate, and raised eyebrows among her fanbase.
articles.body: Vanity Fair published a piece on Taylor Swift Monday that didn't name the pop superstar directly, quoting mostly anonymous sources from her early life and in the music industry, raising eyebrows across her fandom as well as in the media. May Jeong, a Vanity Fair journalist, spoke with more than 100 people for the story and used almost no names at all throughout it. Instead, she referred to Swift as "The Star," and used similar descriptors for others. Some of the people she spoke to were named. The piece was headlined, "The Mastermind," a reference to Swift's track on her "Midnights" album. The story is split up into an "A Side" and a "B Side," and random capitalized letters – seemingly an attempt to mimic the style of Swift's clues for her fans – spell out "Look What You Made Me Do," the title of a track off her "Reputation" album. VANITY FAIR WRITER IGNITES FIRESTORM FRETTING 'ACCOUNTABILITY JOURNALISM' FAILED TO TAKE DOWN JENSEN HUANG Variety's chief music critic, Chris Willman, published a column Tuesday headlined, "Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?" Willman called Monday, the day of the piece's publication, "a bad day for journalism." ESPN’S FAVORITE INSIDER ACCIDENTALLY EXPLAINED WHY MOST AMERICANS DON’T TRUST THE MEDIA The piece names an anonymous industry executive, "The Exec," who refers to Swift as "Regina George," one of the titular "Mean Girls" in the 2004 hit comedy. Swift's team did not return Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Vanity Fair also did not return a request for comment. Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence and former editor-in-chief of People, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "I think Vanity Fair was building a creative framework, and I applaud the ambition. Tina Brown rebuilt the magazine in the 1980s on high-low: serious writing about popular subjects, gossip given a literary treatment. 'The Mastermind' tries the same trick. It takes the most popular star alive and runs her through the oldest format in gossip, the blind item." However, Wakeford argued that the "blind item" format only works when readers really don't know who it is. "Here everybody knows," he continued. "So the device has nothing to hide and just looks timid. Every source hiding behind a code name makes the piece feel unsigned, like nobody wants their fingerprints on it, including the magazine." One of the portions of the article going viral is a former classmate's recollection of Swift wearing Ugg boots at their Pennsylvania school. "She asked her mother for a pair of the same boots. 'Do you know how much they cost?' her mother said. A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother’s paycheck working variously at a bakery, at a dairy mill, and as a caretaker. Peppers recalls The Star owning multiples of Uggs: 'She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one,'" the piece reads. The portion about the Uggs was widely mocked on TikTok and X. LEGACY MEDIA TRUST HITS NEW LOW WITH SWALWELL STORY LATEST EXAMPLE OF PROTECTING DEMS "A profile that never names its subject and leans on more than 100 sources, many anonymous or renamed, asks readers for a lot of trust. When people can't tell who said what, the story stops reading as reporting and starts reading as a grudge. That's why the Ugg boots detail became the meme. It told readers how thin some of the material was," Amore Philip, a communications advisor and founder of Apples & Oranges Public Relations, told Fox News Digital. Philip said that detail became a symbol of the whole piece — which probed Swift's curated image and school background — for a reason. "The Uggs prove the point. Run a woman's teenage boot rotation as evidence and you've told readers how thin the rest is. There's a genuinely moving story about class in that anecdote, and it belongs in a braver article," Philip added. Piers Morgan called out the article on X. "This may be the bitchiest, nastiest hatchet job I’ve ever read in a supposedly elite magazine. From my personal experience and knowledge of @taylorswift13 she is a hard-working, talented, generous and surprisingly down-to-earth woman given her superstardom," he wrote. David Christopher Lee, a celebrity and portrait photographer, as well as an editor-in-chief of David's Guide, said in a statement to Fox News Digital, "A profile built on more than 100 voices, most of them anonymous or renamed, is not a portrait of a person. It is a collage of other people's versions of her, and the subject never gets to answer any of it." Lee added, "I have spent 27 years photographing famous people, and the gap between the person in front of my lens and the person in the coverage is always wide. Anonymous sourcing at this scale does not close that gap. It widens it." Wakeford argued that Vanity Fair told the story with the lights off. "There's a real story in there, which is a shame. Taylor Swift may be the most powerful person in the music business. She moves local economies. She fills the charts so completely that new artists can't get near the top. Power that big deserves scrutiny, and Vanity Fair deserves credit for having some bite again. They finally found a story. Then they told it with the lights off," he said. Swift's fans have also panned the article online. "Swifties are calling it a hit piece, and on the craft they have a point. Real investigative journalism about the powerful does the opposite of this. It names its subject and, wherever possible, its sources, and it shows its working," Wakeford said in the statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Swifties are the most organized reputation management team in entertainment, and Taylor doesn't pay them. Within hours they flipped the question from 'what did she do?' to 'why did Vanity Fair publish this?' That is crisis communications run by the crowd."

articles.title: Mims Davies: People are profiting on my likeness for AI porn
articles.summary: Mims Davies urged people to report any incidents so that “culprits can be held to account”.
articles.body:
A member of parliament whose name and image were used in AI content on porn sites said the issue could make women less likely to want to enter public life.

Mims Davies, the shadow Welsh Secretary, said she received an email in her parliamentary inbox which said "her likeness was found on forums in abusive and pornographic content".

The Conservative frontbencher said people making money from deepfakes was "grotesque", urging people to report it if it happens to them so that "culprits can be held to account".

"It's completely unacceptable, it's a violation and an outrage," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast .

Deepfakes are videos, pictures or audio clips made with artificial intelligence to look real .

It is illegal to share or threaten to share intimate photos or videos of someone without their consent, including through deepfake images.

Davies said she had waived her right to anonymity to call for more resources to find and prosecute culprits.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, said "significant action is being taken to tackle intimate image abuse" but added there was "more to do".

Davies, MP for East Grinstead and Uckfield in East Sussex, said: "There are things you expect to be dealing with these days in public life and frankly this is not it.

"This could be any woman. This could be anyone in politics, in business, or down in your high street.

"We need to be able to protect ourselves from deepfakes."

She added: "This is going to have an effect on our daily lives, on our lifestyles. We need an answer to this.

"There's a problem, a new frontier which we need to battle."

She previously told the BBC she was spiked on a night out in 2019.

Davies, who studied politics and international relations at Swansea University before embarking on a career in journalism in Wales, said the issue was likely to make women "feel less likely to want to enter public life".

"It doesn't just affect you personally, it affects families. You never know when you're walking into a room what people might be thinking.

"We need more women in public life at every single level, from councillors, to Westminster and to the Senedd. It's tough out there.

"We need those kinds of voices in the room."

Her office confirmed reports have been made to the Metropolitan Police and parliamentary authorities.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Nobody should have to experience the trauma of having an explicit deepfake created or shared without their consent.

"Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess and mitigate the risk of UK users encountering illegal content like this on their sites and apps, and remove it quickly when they become aware of it.

"We've laid down clear expectations for how platforms should do this – including by using automated technology to deal with illegal intimate images – and we've driven some of the strongest changes of any online safety regulation in the world.

"We've also shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

In January, Ofcom launched an investigation into X over concerns its AI tool Grok was being used to create sexualised images.

The regulator gave platforms until the end of September this year to take effective steps to stop illegal intimate images and deepfakes from spreading.

articles.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
articles.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
articles.body:
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.

It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.

The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.

Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

articles.title: Chinese scientist, Arizona State University assistant professor, says he does not know why he was arrested by ICE: 'I still have nightmares'
articles.summary: A Chinese-born scientist working in the United States has described the fear and uncertainty he experienced after being arrested by ICE agents despite
articles.body: A Chinese-born scientist working in the United States has described the fear and uncertainty he experienced after being arrested by ICE agents despite having what he believed was a clean immigration record and having followed the rules for years. Di Liu, an assistant professor of chemistry at Arizona State University, was arrested by plainclothes ICE agents at an airport in July while preparing to board a domestic flight from Phoenix to Nashville, Tennessee, to attend an academic conference.Liu told Science he was in an airport bathroom when three men suddenly appeared and blocked his way. The agents identified themselves as immigration officers and arrested him over alleged immigration violations.The scientist initially thought the encounter was a prank. Having moved to the United States from China in 2011 to pursue his PhD, he said he had carefully followed immigration requirements and never expected to be detained.Liu was released on July 28, but said the experience continued to haunt him. "They didn't tell me why. No explanation," he recalled.He said he still experiences nightmares about the arrest and described the incident as a deeply frightening experience.'I was certain they made a mistake'Liu said when he was being handcuffed and taken to a holding room at ICE’s field office in Phoenix, he continued to hope against hope that agents would soon realize they’d made a mistake and let him go. Only when he was transferred to ICE’s immigration jail in the early morning of July 21, two days after his arrest, did he start to panic. “I was wrapped in enormous fear,” he said. “I didn’t know what would happen next and how I ended up here.”Liu’s wife, a physicist at ASU, later told him that when she picked up his call from a jail payphone number, she was suspicious, wondering whether a scammer was using artificial intelligence to mimic his voice.On July 28, Liu was released as mysteriously as he was arrested.Liu’s university had filed a renewal application four months before his visa was set to expire, which used to be enough time for the application to be renewed, but now the waiting time is long and such cases eventually become "visa overstay".Liu said he could not attend the important conference that day where he was scheduled to present his lab's new research. As he was arrested, he also missed some deadlines for grant proposals. The three papers he aimed to publish during the summer were deferred.
